newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian radio says fight for democracy goes on.
newsitem.headline: Croatian radio says fight for democracy goes on.

text.p: A day after 100,000 Croatians rallied to block a government move to shut down an independent radio station, its editors said they faced more battles ahead to secure real democracy.
"What happened yesterday proves the people of Zagreb and Croatia are not going to put up with everything," said Zrinka Vrabec-Mojzes, the charismatic editor-in-chief of Radio 101.
"This number of people was not seen in Zagreb for five years. But we are not so naive to think that this was a final victory," she added.
The peaceful one-hour rally at the main Zagreb square on Thursday evening was called to protest a government bid to shut down the most popular radio station in the capital.

A government-controlled telecommunications council on Wednesday failed to grant the radio a broadcasting licence, which caused an outburst of public rage and foreign protest on a scale that caught the authorities off guard.
The next day, fearful the rally would turn violent, the authorities rowed back and anulled the decision.
They said a new tender would be open but radio managers protested they had already met all requirements to stay on air.

"We are not planning to run for the fourth time for a license we think we deserved after 12 years of work," Vrabec-Mojzes said. "We demand an immediate five-year licence and a stronger transmitter which would be better placed."
The row over the radio split the ruling Croatian Democratic Union.
While a majority of government ministers voiced their support for the radio, top party hawk and member of the telecommunications council Ivic Pasalic attacked the radio.
"Radio 101 is an oppositionist, and not independent media," Pasalic was quoted saying by daily Vecernji List on Thursday.
He appeared to be backed by nationalist President Franjo Tudjman, who is being treated in a Washington military hospital for what U.S. sources said was stomach cancer.

"Look what they are doing to us in Zagreb. 'Dinamo', the return of communism...We are not going to let it happen," Tudjman was quoted as saying privately in Washington by the independent Novi List newspaper.
He was referring to popular calls for the return of the old, communist-era name "Dinamo" for a Zagreb soccer club, which he personally renamed "Croatia" after coming to power.
No other media, most of whom are under tight state and party control, carried the Novi List report.

"With the best wishes for his speedy recovery, I hope the president will have enough political wisdom not to link Radio 101 with communism, when it is well-known that we had actively worked on its demise in the '80s," Vrabec-Mojzes said.
It is unclear if support for Radio 101 will become a wider call for more freedom in a country Tudjman runs with an iron fist.
